data.title: Mikulčice–Kopčany – a Great Moravian centre with twelve churches
data.excerpt: One of the most important fortified centres of Great Moravia: some twelve churches, features of urban organisation and the probable seat of the first Mojmirids. After the collapse of Moravia its remains were left preserved beneath the flood deposits of the Morava, undamaged by later building.

children.text: The Valy site at Mikulčice, or more precisely between Mikulčice and Kopčany, is one of the most important fortified hillfort settlements with features of urban organisation, with evidence of occupation of the pre-Great Moravian and Great Moravian horizons, with a large number of churches (c. 12) and artefacts attesting to the presence of the Great Moravian nobility. There are suggestions that it may have been a tribal centre with higher aspirations to power, perhaps even the seat of the first Mojmirids. After the collapse of old Moravia this fortified town did not develop any further; its remains were left preserved beneath the alluvial deposits of the floods of the Morava, undamaged by later building or human activity, and so it has been possible to form a more comprehensive picture of the life of our ancestors. We do not know the name of this town, but in the 9th century it did not lie on the present-day side of the Morava; instead the river flowed around it, that is, it stood on a kind of island formed by the Morava and its side branches. Some historians state that the main channel of the river ran to the west of the hillfort, and that it therefore lay rather within the territory of present-day Slovakia. Between the main channel of the Morava and the hillfort there were marshes and branches of the river, which thus perfectly protected the fortified town from an enemy approaching from the west. The Morava is said to have changed its course after a large dyke was built below Hodonín, which deflected the river channel eastwards towards Holíč.

Professor Havlík believed that the original name of the town, or rather of the hillfort, was grad Morava, although several researchers favour the name grad Slavníč or Slivnica. Since present-day Kopčany lies roughly the same distance from the hillfort as Mikulčice, I think it is not at all incorrect to use the term the Mikulčice–Kopčany hillfort, or agglomeration. This is best documented by the fact that the small church of St Margaret of Antioch, which stands on the Slovak side in Kopčany, was originally quite clearly part of the hillfort agglomeration.

The area was already occupied in the 7th century, and in the 9th century the hillfort was fortified with ramparts. In the centre of the enclosure stood the acropolis, whose extent is defined by the remains of the ramparts and by the princely palace. Remains of workshops, buildings, the princely palace, a three-aisled basilica and a further 11 churches were found here. In addition there were more than 2,500 graves. The archaeological sites extend over an area of 10 ha.

The agglomeration, as has already been indicated, lies in the floodplain of the Morava, in a landscape of riparian woodland. Its core is formed by the main acropolis already mentioned, with two large adjoining baileys, one of which clearly has the character of a permanent military camp, while the other appears rather to be a settlement protected by a rampart. The slightly elevated acropolis of the Great Moravian stronghold, together with the military bailey, was protected by an almost identical wall of shell construction with a stone front revetment, and by moats formed by the system of branches of the Morava.
Buildings

Among the buildings, particular interest attaches to the three-aisled basilica with an elongated apse closed in a semicircle, two narthexes divided by a partition, a baptistery and a surrounding cemetery (church no. 3), which is the largest Great Moravian religious building known to date, 34 m long and 9 m wide. In five tombs in the nave of the church, unfortunately already robbed, members of the highest Great Moravian ecclesiastical or secular nobility were probably buried. The view has also been put forward that Archbishop Methodius was buried in grave no. 580 in the main nave of the basilica. This conjecture, like the idea of a cathedral church, rests on the so-called Life of Saints Cyril and Methodius, which says that Methodius “lies then in the great church of Moravia, on the left-hand side, in the wall behind the altar of the Holy Mother of God”. Such a burial would have been possible here, because the foundation of the apse is almost 1 m wide. Nothing, however, was found. If there was a grave directly in the wall or in a tomb, then it was undoubtedly destroyed when the stone was quarried away. Nevertheless, the fact that Methodius had a cathedral church is sufficient proof that the ecclesiastical situation in Moravia was already well stabilised.

Around the church 350 graves were discovered, and the finds from them allow us to assume that this church was built soon after the arrival of the Byzantine mission. Evidence of this may also be the find of a “Charon’s coin” — a gold solidus of the Byzantine emperor Michael III dating from 856–866, from the grave of a magnate situated close to the southern foundation wall of the basilica. The position of the basilica too, that is, within the princely stronghold, thus not outside but inside the administrative centre, attests to its function as the bishop’s church at the time the Byzantine mission was active. The architectural type of the Moravian churches with semicircular apses likewise derives from Early Christian church architecture, which was brought to Moravia from Byzantium.

Christianity in the central region of Great Moravia is not demonstrated only by the foundations of church buildings — although the concentration of twelve religious buildings in a relatively small area points to close links between ecclesiastical and political organisation — but also by the more numerous products of local art and craft workshops and by some imported objects connected with Christian symbolism. So far finds of this kind, almost all of them coming from graves, are represented in the greatest numbers at Mikulčice. Among them are a small silver cross, an engraving of a priest, a silver
gombík
with fishes and others.

Another important find is the rotunda with two apses (church no. 6), discovered in 1960, which so far has no parallel in the central region of Great Moravia. It is almost 15 m long and 7.30 m wide. On the basis of objects found in one of the 190 graves that belonged to it, this building can be dated to the first third of the 9th century. The rotunda was decorated with frescoes, fragments of which were found in the debris of the church. Some fragments suggest that the frescoes included the depiction of a human figure. In the vicinity of the basilica metal objects were found, above all iron spurs, which show that alongside craftsmen there also lived at Mikulčice horsemen who formed part of the prince’s retinue.

children.text: At the highest point of the hillfort, fragments of mortar and plaster were identified on the surface. The remains of the foundations of a rectangular building, 26 m long and almost 10 m wide, were discovered. The original foundation masonry survived mainly in the partition that divided the building into an eastern (smaller) and a western (larger) part. The western space of the building was completely destroyed by the inhabitants of the settlement in the 10th and 11th centuries, who built their houses directly on the ruins of the structure. (Here one clearly sees what fate befell those sites where people lived and built continuously up to the present day — Nitra, for example.) Inside the western part, remains of a poured mortar floor and roundwood with stone facing were discovered. Originally there were wooden posts here which carried a flat wooden ceiling. The remains of a stone fireplace were found here. The building was dated to the 9th century. In the first half of the 10th century it came to an end together with the churches. The position of this building at the highest point of the hillfort, its shape and the remains of the stone fireplace lead to the conjecture that these could be the remains of a princely palace. This theory is supported by the fact that the builders of the princely stronghold at Mikulčice and of the magnates’ residences made use not only of the maze of river branches, but also strongly fortified the individual settlement complexes with wooden palisades and walls. Evidence of the presence of an upper stratum is also the larger number of finds of spurs, including gilded ones and iron ones inlaid with silver and copper, as well as the find of a larger number of swords. The secular character of the building is indicated by the remains of the stone fireplace, which one would hardly look for in a church. The remains of the poured mortar floors likewise testify to the above-average quality of the dwelling.
Finds

The cemetery mentioned above, which was discovered in the vicinity of the basilica, stands out for the number of rich graves with swords, gold and silver jewellery, splendid sets of belt mounts, silver and cast bronze strap ends and gold
gombíky

. These and a number of other finds are masterpieces of local artistic craftsmanship. Among the valuable finds are above all a silver pendant cross with the figure of Christ and the gold solidus of the Byzantine emperor Michael III. Finds of iron writing implements, styli, are also a certain testimony to literacy. Traces of metal-casting and jewellery workshops in the stronghold are dated to the period before the middle of the 9th century. In the peak period they disappear and the working of iron and wood, pottery production and textile production predominate. A substantial hinterland also belongs to the agglomeration, including present-day Kopčany mentioned above, with the
Church of St Margaret of Antioch
. The dating of this church, which had rather escaped attention, was made possible by finds of three Great Moravian graves with gilded
gombíky

and silver drum-shaped earrings. Among other interesting finds from the agglomeration one may name the remains of a bridge, dugout boats — monoxyla, baskets for catching fish, a harpoon, iron fish hooks, a wooden bucket, a bucket with decorative fittings, iron buckets inlaid with wood, three different types of battle axe, wooden spoons and ladles, a rope, iron horse bits, sheep shears, an iron scythe, an iron fire-steel, iron axe-shaped currency bars, a lead currency bar, arrowheads, iron keys and lock fittings, bone skates, awls, antler needle cases, fired-clay branch beds, a bone whistle. Particular attention was attracted by a small silver-gilt reliquary in the shape of a miniature liturgical book. An interesting detail is the abundant traces of the consumption of food of all kinds.

Attention should also be paid to the fundamental reconstruction (not mere routine maintenance) of the older stone wall on the Mikulčice ramparts some time in the middle of the 9th century, without any signs of a sudden catastrophe (fire, capture and the like). The rebuilt wall had a markedly less massive stone facing. It looks as though the political importance of the original hillfort declined here, and only after a new ordering of public affairs did new representatives of power see to the renewal of the dilapidated enclosure, though no longer with its former significance and earlier aspirations to power. Professor Poulík’s idea of the centre of the state at Mikulčice therefore does not appear realistic for the peak Great Moravian period, but it could theoretically have applied to the first half of the 9th century.
Kopčany — the Slovak part of Mikulčice

In the Great Moravian period Kopčany took part in the busy life of the Great Moravian centre at Valy, whose core lay within 1.5 km of the farming and herding hamlets situated in the present-day cadastral area of the village. A Great Moravian centre as powerful as Valy would have been unthinkable without a dependent farming population, whose hamlets surrounded Valy over an area of about forty square kilometres. Along the road from the complex of the stronghold centre, Valy, towards Holíč there was a whole series of small agricultural and craft hamlets with cemeteries situated on sandy knolls. From the point of view of current archaeological research it follows that Valy was closer to Kopčany than to present-day Mikulčice, that the only “open gateway” led from the hillfort to the east, i.e. that Valy was more accessible from Kopčany, and by several roads, and so it could be given the epithet the Kopčany–Mikulčice Valy, if not the Kopčany Valy (Štefan Janšák). “The main branch of the Morava flowed three and a quarter kilometres to the west of the Great Moravian fortified town, below the sandy terrace on which the present-day villages of Lužice, Mikulčice and Moravská Nová Ves are spread out. It follows from this that the town at Valy lay on its left bank... the fortified town at Valy gravitated both geographically and economically towards the territory of present-day Slovakia... detailed research has shown that on the line from Valy to the present-day village of Mikulčice there is not a single hamlet of the Great Moravian period, which means that in those times there was a marsh three and a half kilometres wide there” (Š. Janšák — Brány do dávnoveku / Gateways into Antiquity).

children.text: Even after the demise of the Mikulčice hillfort, life continued in the two hamlets known so far in the vicinity of the Church of St Margaret of Antioch until the 13th century, when this area probably became the last inhabited place of the former Mikulčice agglomeration, if we leave aside the remains of medieval occupation around the former church no. 9 in the outer settlement below the Valy hillfort. Research on the historical topography carried out so far suggests that the last inhabitants of the hamlet around the Church of St Margaret of Antioch left, probably for present-day Kopčany, in the 16th–17th centuries. The church probably continued to serve the surrounding area until the 18th century, when a new church was built in the village itself.
